title: Three Numbers From Two Moves: Calibrating the Odometry You Believed

questions.question: A robot with a left wheel 1.2 percent big, a right wheel 0.6 percent small and a wheel base 2 percent wide drives a 16 metre square on odometry that believes the drawing. How far out does it finish?
options: About 250 cm, and 46 degrees out in heading: the three errors add and every straight line is a curve
It finishes exactly, because the errors cancel
questions.explanation: The same in the same direction every time, so averaging does not help. Individually they were 132, 75 and 35 cm.

questions.question: Why does it take two moves and not one to find three numbers?
options: One move is enough with enough accuracy
A straight drive gives two things, the average wheel scale and the difference between the wheels, but only a spin depends on the wheelbase
The second move checks the first
questions.explanation: Three unknowns, and a straight drive tells two of them. The spin is the only move whose rotation depends on how far apart the wheels are.

questions.question: Why are the three numbers found in order: the mean scale, then the wheelbase, then the difference?
options: Each needs the one before: the wheelbase from the spin needs the mean scale, and the difference from the veer needs the real wheelbase
questions.explanation: Solving them in another order has an unknown on the right of every equation.

questions.question: Why can the robot not measure its own straight drive?
options: How far it went is the thing it is wrong about: the encoders say what they say, so the measurement has to come from outside, a tape or a camera
questions.explanation: Which is why a calibration is as good as the tape and the protractor.

questions.question: Twenty calibrations with a tape good to 3 mm and a protractor good to 0.2 degrees gave each scale to about 0.06 percent rms, and the square closed to 2.3 cm. What limits it?
options: The noise in the measurements, which goes into the three numbers; longer test moves make a fixed error a smaller fraction
questions.explanation: A hundred times better than 249.9 cm, and what remains is measurement noise.

questions.question: A robot is calibrated on a dry floor and then drives on a wet one. What is wrong with the calibration?
options: It finds errors that are the same every time; a wheel that slips is a different robot each run, so the calibration is no help and the position needs correcting from outside
questions.explanation: Calibration removes the systematic errors. What is random, or changes with the surface, is what a correction from outside is for.
